questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith (WCF), primarily in **Chapter 8** ("Of Christ the Mediator"), teaches the following core doctrines about Christ:

### 1. Eternal Appointment as Mediator
- It pleased God, in His eternal purpose, to choose and ordain His only begotten Son to be the mediator between God and humanity.
- Christ is the prophet, priest, and king; the head and savior of His church; heir of all things; and judge of the world.
- From eternity, God gave Him a people (the elect) to redeem, call, justify, sanctify, and glorify.

### 2. Two Natures in One Person
- The Son of God, the second person of the Trinity (eternally God, of one substance and equal with the Father), assumed human nature with all its essential properties and common infirmities—yet without sin.
- He was conceived by the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin Mary, of her substance.
- These two whole, perfect, and distinct natures (divine and human) are inseparably united in one person, without confusion, mixture, or separation.
- Thus, He is truly God and truly man, the only mediator between God and man.

### 3. Offices and Work
- Christ was anointed with the Holy Spirit and equipped for His mediatorial office.
- As **prophet**, He reveals God’s will.
- As **priest**, He offered Himself once as a sacrifice and continually intercedes.
- As **king**, He rules over all things for the church’s good.

### 4. Humiliation and Exaltation
- In His state of humiliation, He was born under the law, perfectly obeyed it, suffered the wrath of God, was crucified, died, was buried, and remained under death’s power (though without corruption).
- In His exaltation, He rose on the third day, ascended into heaven, sits at the Father’s right hand, and will return to judge the world.

### 5. Redemption Applied
- By His perfect obedience and sacrifice, Christ purchased reconciliation with God and eternal life for all the elect.
- He effectually applies this redemption to them through His Word and Spirit, granting faith, justification, sanctification, and perseverance.

This chapter emphasizes that Christ’s mediation is rooted in God’s sovereign decree, accomplished through His unique person and work, and applied only to those given to Him by the Father.

questions.question: What does the Westminster Confession of Faith teach about effectual calling?
questions.reference_answer: All those whom God hath predestinated unto life, and those only, he is pleased, in his appointed and accepted time, effectually to call, by his Word and Spirit, out of that state of sin and death, in which they are by nature, to grace and salvation by Jesus Christ; enlightening their minds, spiritually and savingly, to understand the things of God; taking away their heart of stone, and giving unto them an heart of flesh; renewing their wills, and by his almighty power determining them to that which is good, and effectually drawing them to Jesus Christ; yet so as they come most freely, being made willing by his grace. This effectual call is of God's free and special grace alone, not from anything at all foreseen in man; who is altogether passive therein, until, being quickened and renewed by the Holy Spirit, he is thereby enabled to answer this call, and to embrace the grace offered and conveyed in it. Elect infants, dying in infancy, are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who worketh when, and where, and how he pleaseth. So also are all other elect persons who are incapable of being outwardly called by the ministry of the Word. Others, not elected, although they may be called by the ministry of the Word, and may have some common operations of the Spirit, yet they never truly come unto Christ, and therefore cannot be saved: much less can men, not professing the Christian religion, be saved in any other way whatsoever, be they never so diligent to frame their lives according to the light of nature and the law of that religion they do profess; and to assert and maintain that they may is very pernicious, and to be detested.

questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith (WCF), Chapter 10, teaches that **effectual calling** is God’s sovereign, gracious, and irresistible work by which He brings the elect out of their natural state of sin and death into salvation through Christ. It is monergistic (accomplished by God alone) and is distinguished from the general or ineffectual call of the gospel that goes out to all people.

Here are the key points of its teaching:

### 1. Only the Elect Are Effectually Called
God effectually calls *only* those whom He has predestinated to life. This calling occurs at the time He has appointed and is accomplished by the Word and Spirit.

> “All those whom God hath predestinated unto life, and those only, He is pleased, in His appointed and accepted time, effectually to call, by His Word and Spirit…” (10.1)

### 2. What Effectual Calling Does
In this calling, God:
- Enlightens the mind spiritually and savingly.
- Removes the heart of stone and gives a heart of flesh.
- Renews the will.
- By His almighty power, makes the person willing and draws them to Christ.

The person comes “most freely,” but only because grace has made them willing. Until the Holy Spirit quickens and renews them, they are passive in the process.

### 3. It Is Entirely of Grace, Not Based on Anything in Man
Effectual calling flows solely from God’s “free and special grace,” not from anything foreseen in the person (faith, works, or responsiveness). Man contributes nothing to the initiation of this call.

### 4. Applies to Elect Infants and Others Incapable of Hearing the Word
Elect infants who die in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit. The same is true of all other elect persons who are incapable of being outwardly called by the preaching of the Word (10.3).

### 5. The Non-Elect May Receive an Outward Call but Not an Effectual One
Those who are not elect may hear the gospel and even experience some common (non-saving) operations of the Spirit, but they never truly come to Christ and therefore cannot be saved. Salvation is impossible apart from this effectual calling (10.4).

### Summary of the Confession’s Doctrine
Effectual calling is the sovereign work of God that actually brings the elect to saving faith and union with Christ. It is not merely an invitation that humans can accept or reject by their own power; it is an effectual summons that overcomes human resistance and infallibly results in salvation for those chosen in Christ.

This chapter stands in the broader Reformed ordo salutis (order of salvation) between predestination (Ch. 3) and justification (Ch. 11).

questions.question: What does the Westminster Confession of Faith teach about justification?
questions.reference_answer: Those whom God effectually calleth he also freely justifieth; not by infusing righteousness into them, but by pardoning their sins, and by accounting and accepting their persons as righteous: not for anything wrought in them, or done by them, but for Christ's sake alone; nor by imputing faith itself, the act of believing, or any other evangelical obedience to them, as their righteousness; but by imputing the obedience and satisfaction of Christ unto them, they receiving and resting on him and his righteousness by faith; which faith they have not of themselves, it is the gift of God. Faith, thus receiving and resting on Christ and his righteousness, is the alone instrument of justification; yet is it not alone in the person justified, but is ever accompanied with all other saving graces, and is no dead faith, but worketh by love. Christ, by his obedience and death, did fully discharge the debt of all those that are thus justified, and did make a proper, real, and full satisfaction to his Father's justice in their behalf. Yet inasmuch as he was given by the Father for them, and his obedience and satisfaction accepted in their stead, and both freely, not for anything in them, their justification is only of free grace; that both the exact justice and rich grace of God might be glorified in the justification of sinners. God did, from all eternity, decree to justify all the elect, and Christ did, in the fulness of time, die for their sins, and rise again for their justification: nevertheless, they are not justified until the Holy Spirit doth, in due time, actually apply Christ unto them. God doth continue to forgive the sins of those that are justified; and although they can never fall from the state of justification, yet they may by their sins fall under God's fatherly displeasure, and not have the light of his countenance restored unto them, until they humble themselves, confess their sins, beg pardon, and renew their faith and repentance. The justification of believers under the Old Testament was, in all these respects, one and the same with the justification of believers under the New Testament.

questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith (WCF), Chapter 11, teaches that justification is a single, forensic (legal) act of God’s free grace, not an ongoing process or infusion of righteousness. It consists in the pardon of all sins and the acceptance of the sinner as perfectly righteous in God’s sight, solely on the basis of Christ’s obedience and satisfaction being imputed to the believer. The key elements are:
- **Ground**: Christ’s active and passive obedience (his righteousness and atoning death) is imputed to the elect; nothing in or done by the sinner contributes to this righteousness.
- **Instrument**: Faith alone receives and rests upon Christ and his righteousness. Faith is not itself the righteousness, nor is it reckoned as such; it is simply the empty hand that apprehends Christ.
- **Subjects**: Only those whom God has effectually called (the elect) are justified. This occurs at different times in their lives but is the same in nature for all.
- **Permanence**: Once justified, believers remain perfectly righteous in Christ and can never fall from that state, though their sins grieve the Holy Spirit, wound their consciences, and interrupt their sense of God’s favor until they repent.
- **Relation to works and sanctification**: Justification is distinguished from sanctification. Good works are the necessary fruit and evidence of justifying faith but play no part in procuring justification itself.
The Confession explicitly rejects Roman Catholic views of infused righteousness, merit, or justification by works, as well as any notion that faith is counted as righteousness in itself. It affirms that justification is received by faith alone, yet that faith is never alone in the person justified—it is always accompanied by other saving graces.

questions.question: What does the Westminster Confession of Faith teach about the perseverance of the saints?
questions.reference_answer: They whom God hath accepted in his Beloved, effectually called and sanctified by his Spirit, can neither totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace; but shall certainly persevere therein to the end, and be eternally saved. This perseverance of the saints depends, not upon their own free will, but upon the immutability of the decree of election, flowing from the free and unchangeable love of God the Father; upon the efficacy of the merit and intercession of Jesus Christ; the abiding of the Spirit and of the seed of God within them; and the nature of the covenant of grace: from all which ariseth also the certainty and infallibility thereof. questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith (Chapter 17, “Of the Perseverance of the Saints”) teaches that those whom God has accepted in Christ, effectually called, and sanctified by his Spirit can neither totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace. They shall certainly persevere to the end and be eternally saved.

This perseverance does not rest on the believer’s own free will or efforts. It rests on:
- the immutability of God’s decree of election,
- the efficacy of Christ’s merit and intercession,
- the abiding presence and work of the Holy Spirit, and
- the unbreakable nature of the covenant of grace.

These grounds make the perseverance of the saints both certain and infallible.

At the same time, the Confession acknowledges that true believers may, through the temptations of Satan and the world, the remaining corruption in them, and neglect of the means of grace, fall into grievous sins and continue in them for a time. Such falls bring God’s fatherly displeasure, the grieving of the Spirit, loss of comfort and assurance, a hardened heart, wounded conscience, harm to others, and temporal judgments—yet they do not result in the loss of saving grace or final apostasy.

In short, the WCF affirms the classic Reformed doctrine that the elect are preserved by God’s sovereign power and will infallibly reach final salvation, even though they may experience serious and painful lapses along the way.

questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith addresses the last judgment primarily in **Chapter 33** ("Of the Last Judgment"). Its teaching can be summarized as follows:

### 1. A definite future day of judgment
God has appointed a specific day on which He will judge the world in righteousness through Jesus Christ, to whom all authority to judge has been given by the Father. On that day:
- Both fallen angels and all human beings who have ever lived will appear before Christ’s judgment seat.
- Every person will give an account of their thoughts, words, and deeds done in the body.
- Judgment will be rendered “according to what they have done in the body, whether good or evil.”

### 2. Purpose of the judgment
The day is appointed for the public manifestation of God’s glory:
- **Mercy**: The eternal salvation of the elect will be openly displayed.
- **Justice**: The damnation of the reprobate (the wicked and disobedient) will be openly displayed.

### 3. The two eternal outcomes
- The righteous will enter into everlasting life and receive “that fulness of joy and refreshing, which shall come from the presence of the Lord.”
- The wicked, who do not know God and do not obey the gospel, will be cast into eternal torments and punished with “everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of His power.”

### 4. Pastoral and practical implications
The Confession teaches that Christ intends believers to be firmly convinced of this coming judgment for two reasons:
- To deter all people from sin.
- To give greater consolation to the godly amid suffering and adversity.

At the same time, the exact timing of the day remains hidden from humanity so that believers will remain watchful, spiritually prepared, and free from carnal security—always ready to say, “Come, Lord Jesus.”

This teaching is consistent with the broader Reformed understanding of the final judgment as a public, universal, and irreversible event that vindicates God’s justice and mercy while bringing history to its appointed consummation.

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the sufficiency of scripture?
questions.reference_answer: We believe that this Holy Scripture contains the will of God completely and that everything one must believe to be saved is sufficiently taught in it. For since the entire manner of service which God requires of us is described in it at great length, no one- even an apostle or an angel from heaven, as Paul says- (Gal. 1:8) ought to teach other than what the Holy Scriptures have already taught us. For since it is forbidden to add to the Word of God, or take anything away from it, (Deut. 12:32, Rev. 22:18-19) it is plainly demonstrated that the teaching is perfect and complete in all respects. Therefore we must not consider human writings- no matter how holy their authors may have been- equal to the divine writings; nor may we put custom, nor the majority, nor age, nor the passage of times or persons, nor councils, decrees, or official decisions above the truth of God, for truth is above everything else. For all human beings are liars by nature and more vain than vanity itself. Therefore we reject with all our hearts everything that does not agree with this infallible rule, as we are taught to do by the apostles when they say, "Test the spirits to see whether they are from God," (1 John 4:1) and also, "Do not receive into the house or welcome anyone who comes to you and does not bring this teaching." (2 John 10)

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession (1561), one of the Three Forms of Unity in Reformed theology, addresses the sufficiency of Scripture most directly in **Article 7**, titled “The Sufficiency of the Holy Scriptures to Be the Only Rule of Faith.”

### Key Teaching (Article 7)

The confession states that the Bible contains everything necessary for salvation and godly living, so that nothing else may be added to or subtracted from it:

> “We believe that those Holy Scriptures fully contain the will of God, and that whatsoever man ought to believe unto salvation is sufficiently taught therein. For since the whole manner of worship which God requires of us is written in them at large, it is unlawful for any one, though an apostle, to teach otherwise than we are now taught in the Holy Scriptures: nay, though it were an angel from heaven, as the apostle Paul says. For since it is forbidden to add unto or take away anything from the Word of God, it does thereby evidently appear that the doctrine thereof is most perfect and complete in all respects.”

It goes on to reject any authority that would supplement or override Scripture:

> “Therefore we reject with all our hearts whatsoever does not agree with this infallible rule.”

### Summary of the Confession’s Doctrine

- **Sufficiency**: Scripture is complete and perfect for faith and practice. Everything a person needs to know for salvation and worship is already contained in it.
- **Sola Scriptura**: No tradition, council, creed, or human writing may be placed on the same level as Scripture. Any teaching that contradicts or adds to the Bible is to be rejected.
- **Clarity and finality**: Because the Scriptures are sufficient, believers do not need additional revelations, ongoing prophetic words, or ecclesiastical traditions to supplement what God has already revealed.

### Related Context in the Belgic Confession

- **Articles 2–5** establish that God reveals Himself both through creation (general revelation) and especially through Scripture (special revelation), and they affirm the canonical books of the Old and New Testaments as the authoritative Word of God.
- **Article 7** then functions as the practical outworking of that revelation: because Scripture is God’s complete Word, it alone is the final authority.

In short, the Belgic Confession teaches that Scripture is **fully sufficient**—nothing more is needed, and nothing may be added.

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the creation of all things?
questions.reference_answer: We believe that the Father, when it seemed good to him, created heaven and earth and all other creatures from nothing, by the Word- that is to say, by the Son. God has given all creatures their being, form, and appearance and their various functions for serving their Creator. Even now God also sustains and governs them all, according to his eternal providence and by his infinite power, that they may serve humanity, in order that humanity may serve God. God has also created the angels good, that they might be messengers of God and serve the elect. Some of them have fallen from the excellence in which God created them into eternal perdition; and the others have persisted and remained in their original state, by the grace of God. The devils and evil spirits are so corrupt that they are enemies of God and of everything good. They lie in wait for the church and every member of it like thieves, with all their power, to destroy and spoil everything by their deceptions. So then, by their own wickedness they are condemned to everlasting damnation, daily awaiting their torments. For that reason we detest the error of the Sadducees, who deny that there are spirits and angels, and also the error of the Manicheans, who say that the devils originated by themselves, being evil by nature, without having been corrupted.

- Each creature was given its own distinct being, form, shape, and appointed role or office so that it might serve its Creator.

The article also notes that God created the angels good, to serve as his messengers and to minister to the elect; some later fell into everlasting perdition, while the rest remained steadfast by grace.

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the doctrine of god's providence?
questions.reference_answer: We believe that this good God, after creating all things, did not abandon them to chance or fortune but leads and governs them according to his holy will, in such a way that nothing happens in this world without God's orderly arrangement. Yet God is not the author of, and cannot be charged with, the sin that occurs. For God's power and goodness are so great and incomprehensible that God arranges and does his works very well and justly even when the devils and the wicked act unjustly. We do not wish to inquire with undue curiosity into what God does that surpasses human understanding and is beyond our ability to comprehend. But in all humility and reverence we adore the just judgments of God, which are hidden from us, being content to be Christ's disciples, so as to learn only what God shows us in the Word, without going beyond those limits. This doctrine gives us unspeakable comfort since it teaches us that nothing can happen to us by chance but only by the arrangement of our gracious heavenly Father, who watches over us with fatherly care, sustaining all creatures under his lordship, so that not one of the hairs on our heads (for they are all numbered) nor even a little bird can fall to the ground without the will of our Father. (Matt. 10:29-30) In this thought we rest, knowing that God holds in check the devils and all our enemies, who cannot hurt us without divine permission and will. For that reason we reject the damnable error of the Epicureans, who say that God does not get involved in anything and leaves everything to chance.

scoring.rubric: Must address the key points of Article 13 (The Doctrine of God's Providence). Should align with the Belgic Confession's teaching on this topic.

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession addresses the doctrine of God’s providence primarily in **Article 13**, titled “The Providence of God.” Here is a clear summary of what it teaches:
### Core Teaching
- After creating all things, God did not abandon them or hand them over to chance or fortune. Instead, He **upholds and governs** all things by His eternal providence and infinite power, according to His holy will.
- Nothing happens in the world “without His appointment.” Even seemingly random or secondary causes are ultimately under God’s sovereign direction.
### Relation to Evil and Sin
The Confession carefully distinguishes God’s providence from being the author of evil:
- God is **not** the author of sin.
- Sin and evil occur because God **permits** them.
- Yet even in permitting sin, God sovereignly restrains it and **overrules** it so that it ultimately serves His good purposes.
### Pastoral Purpose
The article emphasizes the **comfort** this doctrine brings to believers:
- Because nothing happens outside God’s fatherly hand, Christians can be assured that no adversity or evil can separate them from God’s love.
- At the same time, the Confession warns against prying into God’s “secret decrees.” It says we should not try to investigate what God has not revealed, but instead focus on what He has clearly made known in Scripture.
### Summary Statement from Article 13
> “We believe that the same God, after He had created all things, did not forsake them, or give them up to fortune or chance, but that He rules and governs them according to His holy will, so that nothing happens in this world without His appointment…”
In short, the Belgic Confession presents God’s providence as **sovereign, wise, and comforting**, while carefully guarding against both fatalism and the idea that God is responsible for sin.

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the creation and fall of humanity?
questions.reference_answer: We believe that God created human beings from the dust of the earth and made and formed them in his image and likeness- good, just, and holy; able by their will to conform in all things to the will of God. But when they were in honor they did not understand it (Ps. 49:20) and did not recognize their excellence. But they subjected themselves willingly to sin and consequently to death and the curse, lending their ear to the word of the devil. For they transgressed the commandment of life, which they had received, and by their sin they separated themselves from God, who was their true life, having corrupted their entire nature. So they made themselves guilty and subject to physical and spiritual death, having become wicked, perverse, and corrupt in all their ways. They lost all their excellent gifts which they had received from God, and retained none of them except for small traces which are enough to make them inexcusable. Moreover, all the light in us is turned to darkness, as the Scripture teaches us: "The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it." (John 1:5) Here John calls the human race "darkness." Therefore we reject everything taught to the contrary concerning human free will, since humans are nothing but the slaves of sin and cannot do a thing unless it is given them from heaven. (John 3:27) For who can boast of being able to do anything good by oneself, since Christ says, "No one can come to me unless drawn by the Father who sent me"? (John 6:44) Who can glory in their own will when they understand that "the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God"? (Rom. 8:7) Who can speak of their own knowledge in view of the fact that "those who are unspiritual do not receive the gifts of God's Spirit"? (1 Cor. 2:14) In short, who can produce a single thought, knowing that we are not able to think a thing about ourselves, by ourselves, but that "our competence is from God"? (2 Cor. 3:5) And therefore, what the apostle says ought rightly to stand fixed and firm: God works within us both to will and to do according to his good pleasure. (Phil. 2:13) For there is no understanding nor will conforming to God's understanding and will apart from Christ's involvement, as he teaches us when he says, "Apart from me you can do nothing." (John 15:5)

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession (1561) addresses humanity’s creation and fall primarily in Articles 14 and 15 (with supporting material in Article 12 on creation in general). Its teaching may be summarized as follows:
**Creation of humanity (Art. 14)**
God formed man “of the dust of the earth” and “breathed into his nostrils the breath of life,” so that man became a living soul. He was created “in the image of God,” upright, holy, and righteous, possessing true knowledge of God, righteousness, and holiness, and fully capable of willing and doing what is good in conformity with God’s will.
**The Fall (Art. 14)**
Through the instigation of the devil, man “willfully subjected himself to sin” by transgressing the commandment of God. As a result:
- He separated himself from God, who is the true life.
- He corrupted his whole nature.
- He lost all the excellent gifts he had received (including the image of God in its moral and spiritual dimensions).
- He became subject to death, misery, and every kind of evil.
**Original sin and its consequences (Art. 15)**
The corruption introduced by Adam’s fall is transmitted to all his descendants by ordinary generation. This “original sin” is:
- A hereditary depravity and corruption of the entire human nature.
- Sufficient in itself to condemn the whole human race, even infants.
- Not destroyed or fully removed by baptism (though its guilt is forgiven for believers).
- The source of all actual sins throughout life.
Because of this fall, unregenerate humanity is incapable of doing any true spiritual good and is wholly inclined to evil, unless regenerated by the Holy Spirit.
In short, the Belgic Confession presents humanity as originally created good and God-like, but now universally fallen, totally depraved, and in need of sovereign grace for any restoration.

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the doctrine of original sin?
questions.reference_answer: We believe that by the disobedience of Adam original sin has been spread through the whole human race. (Rom. 5:12-13) It is a corruption of the whole human nature- an inherited depravity which even infects small infants in their mother's womb, and the root which produces in humanity every sort of sin. It is therefore so vile and enormous in God's sight that it is enough to condemn the human race, and it is not abolished or wholly uprooted even by baptism, seeing that sin constantly boils forth as though from a contaminated spring. Nevertheless, it is not imputed to God's children for their condemnation but is forgiven by his grace and mercy- not to put them to sleep but so that the awareness of this corruption might often make believers groan as they long to be set free from the body of this death. (Rom. 7:24) Therefore we reject the error of the Pelagians who say that this sin is nothing else than a matter of imitation.

questions.response:
**The Belgic Confession (1561), Article 15 (“Of Original Sin”), teaches the following about original sin:**

- It is the consequence of Adam’s disobedience and is therefore propagated to the entire human race by ordinary generation.
- It consists in a total corruption of human nature—an “hereditary disease” that infects every person from conception (including infants in the womb).
- This corruption is the root and source of all actual sins; it renders humanity incapable of any saving good and inclined to every evil.
- It is so heinous in God’s sight that it alone is sufficient to condemn the whole human race.
- Baptism does not remove or eradicate it; the sinful nature remains and continues to produce actual transgressions throughout life.
- Nevertheless, for those who are in Christ the guilt of original sin is forgiven by grace and is not imputed to their condemnation; yet the remaining corruption should continually humble believers and cause them to long for final deliverance from “this body of death.”

In short, the Belgic Confession presents original sin as both a universal, inherited depravity that justly condemns and as a remaining reality in the believer that is covered by grace but not yet fully eradicated.

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the doctrine of election?
questions.reference_answer: We believe that- all Adam's descendants having thus fallen into perdition and ruin by the sin of Adam- God showed himself to be as he is: merciful and just. God is merciful in withdrawing and saving from this perdition those who, in the eternal and unchangeable divine counsel, have been elected and chosen in Jesus Christ our Lord by his pure goodness, without any consideration of their works. God is just in leaving the others in their ruin and fall into which they plunged themselves.

scoring.rubric: Must address the key points of Article 16 (The Doctrine of Election). Should align with the Belgic Confession's teaching on this topic.

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession (1561) addresses the doctrine of election primarily in **Article 16** (“Of Eternal Election”), with related statements appearing in Articles 12 (providence), 13, and 20–21. Its teaching may be summarized as follows:

- All humanity fell into sin and ruin through Adam’s transgression.  
- Out of this fallen mass God sovereignly and graciously elects some to salvation. This election occurs “in Christ Jesus our Lord” according to God’s “eternal and immutable counsel” and rests solely on His “mere goodness,” with no regard to foreseen faith, works, or merit.  
- Those not elected are left in their sin and perdition; this is presented as an act of divine justice rather than an arbitrary decree.  
- The elect are preserved and delivered by God’s mercy; the non-elect remain under the just consequences of their own fall.

The Confession therefore affirms unconditional, gracious election in Christ while simultaneously acknowledging reprobation as the just “leaving” of the rest of humanity in the ruin they have brought upon themselves. It does not develop the doctrine at the length later found in the Canons of Dort (1618–19), but it clearly places election within the framework of God’s sovereign mercy and justice rather than human decision or foreseen merit.

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the righteousness of faith?
questions.reference_answer: We believe that for us to acquire the true knowledge of this great mystery the Holy Spirit kindles in our hearts a true faith that embraces Jesus Christ, with all his merits, and makes him its own, and no longer looks for anything apart from him. For it must necessarily follow that either all that is required for our salvation is not in Christ or, if all is in him, then those who have Christ by faith have his salvation entirely. Therefore, to say that Christ is not enough but that something else is needed as well is a most enormous blasphemy against God- for it then would follow that Jesus Christ is only half a Savior. And therefore we justly say with Paul that we are justified "by faith alone" or "by faith apart from works." (Rom. 3:28) However, we do not mean, properly speaking, that it is faith itself that justifies us- for faith is only the instrument by which we embrace Christ, our righteousness. But Jesus Christ is our righteousness in making available to us all his merits and all the holy works he has done for us and in our place. And faith is the instrument that keeps us in communion with him and with all his benefits. When those benefits are made ours, they are more than enough to absolve us of our sins.

scoring.rubric: Must address the key points of Article 22 (The Righteousness of Faith). Should align with the Belgic Confession's teaching on this topic.

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession (1561), one of the Three Forms of Unity, addresses the righteousness of faith primarily in Articles 22–24. It teaches that this righteousness is not inherent in the believer or produced by faith as a work, but is the perfect obedience and satisfaction of Christ alone, imputed (credited) to the sinner and received solely by faith as the instrument.

Key points include:
- Justification consists in the forgiveness of sins and the imputation of Christ’s righteousness, so that the believer is declared righteous before God on the basis of Christ’s merits alone (Art. 23).
- Faith itself does not justify; it is merely the empty hand or instrument by which the believer embraces and receives Christ’s righteousness (Art. 22).
- No human works, merits, or partial righteousness contribute to justification; all glory belongs to God, and the believer rests entirely on Christ’s obedience (Art. 22–23).
- This justification by faith produces good works as its fruit, but those works are never the ground of righteousness (Art. 24).

In short, the Confession affirms the classic Reformed doctrine of justification by faith alone (*sola fide*), with Christ’s imputed righteousness as its sole basis.

Final answer: Christ’s imputed righteousness received by faith alone (Arts. 22–24)

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the last judgement?
questions.reference_answer: Finally we believe, according to God's Word, that when the time appointed by the Lord is come (which is unknown to all creatures) and the number of the elect is complete, our Lord Jesus Christ will come from heaven, bodily and visibly, as he ascended, with great glory and majesty, to declare himself the judge of the living and the dead. He will burn this old world, in fire and flame, in order to cleanse it. Then all human creatures will appear in person before the great judge- men, women, and children, who have lived from the beginning until the end of the world. They will be summoned there "with the archangel's call and with the sound of God's trumpet." (1 Thess. 4:16) For all those who died before that time will be raised from the earth, their spirits being joined and united with their own bodies in which they lived. And as for those who are still alive, they will not die like the others but will be changed "in the twinkling of an eye" from perishable to imperishable. (1 Cor. 15:51-53) Then the books (that is, the consciences) will be opened, and the dead will be judged according to the things they did in the world, (Rev. 20:12) whether good or evil. Indeed, all people will give account of all the idle words they have spoken, (Matt. 12:36) which the world regards as only playing games. And then the secrets and hypocrisies of all people will be publicly uncovered in the sight of all. Therefore, with good reason the thought of this judgment is horrible and dreadful to wicked and evil people. But it is very pleasant and a great comfort to the righteous and elect, since their total redemption will then be accomplished. They will then receive the fruits of their labor and of the trouble they have suffered; their innocence will be openly recognized by all; and they will see the terrible vengeance that God will bring on the evil ones who tyrannized, oppressed, and tormented them in this world. The evil ones will be convicted by the witness of their own consciences, and shall be made immortal- but only to be tormented in "the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels." (Matt. 25:41) In contrast, the faithful and elect will be crowned with glory and honor. The Son of God will profess their names (Matt. 10:32) before God his Father and the holy and elect angels; all tears will be wiped from their eyes; (Rev. 7:17) and their cause- at present condemned as heretical and evil by many judges and civil officers- will be acknowledged as the cause of the Son of God. And as a gracious reward the Lord will make them possess a glory such as the human heart could never imagine. So we look forward to that great day with longing in order to enjoy fully the promises of God in Christ Jesus, our Lord.

scoring.rubric: Must address the key points of Article 37 (The Last Judgement). Should align with the Belgic Confession's teaching on this topic.

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession addresses the Last Judgment primarily in **Article 37** (“The Last Judgment”), with supporting statements in Articles 18, 19, and 31. Its teaching can be summarized as follows:

### 1. Christ’s Visible Return and the General Resurrection
- At the appointed time, Jesus Christ will return visibly and bodily from heaven “with great glory and majesty” to judge the living and the dead.
- All the dead will be raised: the bodies of both believers and unbelievers will be reunited with their souls so that the whole person stands before Christ.

### 2. Universal Accountability
- Every person will appear before Christ’s judgment seat.
- The “books will be opened,” and judgment will be rendered “according to what each one has done in the body, whether good or evil” (reflecting 2 Corinthians 5:10 and Revelation 20:12).
- Even the secrets of the heart will be disclosed, so that God’s justice is publicly vindicated.

### 3. Twofold Outcome
- **The righteous (believers)**: Those who have trusted in Christ alone for salvation will be publicly acquitted and received into eternal life and glory. Their good works, done in faith, serve as evidence of genuine faith rather than the ground of their acceptance.
- **The wicked (unbelievers)**: Those who have rejected Christ will be condemned to everlasting punishment, separated from God forever.

### 4. Purpose of the Judgment
The final judgment is not merely punitive; it is the public manifestation of God’s perfect justice and mercy. It brings to completion the salvation accomplished by Christ and the vindication of all who have suffered for righteousness’ sake.

In short, the Belgic Confession presents the Last Judgment as a future, public, universal event in which the risen Christ will judge every person according to works, resulting in the eternal blessedness of believers and the eternal condemnation of unbelievers.

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about the holy scriptures?
questions.reference_answer: The Holy Scripture is the only sufficient, certain, and infallible rule of all saving Knowledge, Faith and Obedience; Although the light of Nature, and the works of Creation and Providence do so far manifest the goodness, wisdom and power of God, as to leave men unexcusable; yet are they not sufficient to give that knowledge of God and His will, which is necessary unto Salvation. Therefore it pleased the Lord at sundry times, and in divers manners, to reveal himself, and to declare that His will unto his Church; and afterward for the better preserving, and propagating of the Truth, and for the more sure Establishment, and Comfort of the Church against the corruption of the flesh, and the malice of Satan, and of the World, to commit the same wholly unto writing; which maketh the Holy Scriptures to be most necessary, those former ways of Gods revealing his will unto his people being now ceased. Under the Name of Holy Scripture or the Word of God written; are now contained all the Books of the Old and New Testament which are these: Of the Old Testament: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, The Song of Songs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi. Of the New Testament: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, The Acts of the Apostles, Pauls Epistle to the Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Phillippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, to Titus, to Philemon, the Epistle to the Hebrews, the Epistle of James, the First and Second Epistles of Peter, the First, Second and Third Epistles of John, the Epistle of Jude, the Revelation. The Books commonly called Apocrypha not being of Divine inspiration, are no part of the Canon (or rule) of the Scripture, and therefore are of no authority to the Church of God, nor to be any otherwise approved or made use of, then other humane writings. The Authority of the Holy Scripture for which it ought to be believed dependeth not upon the testimony of any man, or Church; but wholly upon God (who is truth it self) the Author thereof; therefore it is to be received, because it is the Word of God. We may be moved and induced by the testimony of the Church of God, to an high and reverent esteem of the Holy Scriptures; and the heavenliness of the matter, the efficacy of the Doctrine, and the Majesty of the stile, the consent of all the parts, the scope of the whole (which is to give all glory to God) the full discovery it makes of the only way of mans salvation, and many other incomparable Excellencies, and intire perfections thereof, are arguments whereby it doth abundantly evidence it self to be the Word of God; yet notwithstanding; our full perswasion, and assurance of the infallible truth, and divine authority thereof, is from the inward work of the Holy Spirit, bearing witness by and with the Word in our Hearts. The whole Councel of God concerning all things necessary for his own Glory, Mans Salvation, Faith and Life, is either expressely set down or necessarily contained in the Holy Scripture; unto which nothing at any time is to be added, whether by new Revelation of the Spirit, or traditions of men.Nevertheless we acknowledge the inward illumination of the Spirit of God, to be necessary for the saving understanding of such things as are revealed in the Word, and that there are some circumstances concerning the worship of God, and government of the Church common to humane actions and societies; which are to be ordered by the light of nature, and Christian prudence according to the general rules of the Word, which are always to be observed. All things in Scripture are not alike plain in themselves, nor alike clear unto all; yet those things which are necessary to be known, believed, and observed for Salvation, are so clearly propounded, and opened in some place of Scripture or other, that not only the learned, but the unlearned, in a due use of ordinary means, may attain to a sufficient understanding of them. The Old Testament in Hebrew, (which was the Native language of the people of God of old) and the New Testament in Greek (which at the time of the writing of it was most generally known to the Nations being immediately inspired by God, and by his singular care and Providence kept pure in all Ages, are therefore authentical; so as in all controversies of Religion the Church is finally to appeal unto them But because these original tongues are not known to all the people of God, who have a right unto, and interest in the Scriptures, and are commanded in the fear of God to read and search them, therefore they are to be translated into the vulgar language of every Nation, unto which they come, that the Word of God dwelling plentifully in all, they may worship him in an acceptable manner, and through patience and comfort of the Scriptures may have hope. The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture it self: And therefore when there is a question about the true and full sense of any Scripture (which is not manifold but one) it must be searched by other places that speak more clearly. The supream judge by which all controversies of Religion are to be determined, and all Decrees of Councels, opinions of antient Writers, Doctrines of men, and private Spirits, are to be examined, and in whose sentence we are to rest, can be no other but the Holy Scripture delivered by the Spirit, into which Scripture so delivered, our faith is finally resolved.

questions.response:
The 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith addresses the doctrine of Scripture primarily in its first chapter (“Of the Holy Scriptures”). Its teaching can be summarized under several key headings drawn directly from the document:

- **Sole and sufficient authority**  
  Scripture is declared to be “the only sufficient, certain, and infallible rule of all saving knowledge, faith, and obedience” (1.1). Nothing else—tradition, church pronouncements, or new revelations—may be added to or set alongside it as a rule for Christian faith and life.

- **Divine inspiration and canon**  
  All sixty-six books of the Protestant canon (explicitly listed in 1.2) are “given by inspiration of God” and are therefore the Word of God written. The Apocrypha is explicitly excluded from the canon (1.3).

- **Divine, not ecclesiastical, authority**  
  The authority of Scripture “dependeth not upon the testimony of any man or church, but wholly upon God (who is truth itself), the author thereof” (1.4). While the church’s testimony may be useful, the ultimate ground of belief is the self-authenticating character of God’s Word.

- **Sufficiency**  
  The whole counsel of God concerning all things necessary for salvation, faith, and life is “either expressly set down or necessarily contained” in Scripture (1.6). Nothing is to be added by new revelations or traditions.

- **Clarity (perspicuity)**  
  Although not everything in Scripture is equally plain, “those things which are necessary to be known, believed, and observed for salvation” are clearly set forth, so that both the learned and the unlearned may attain sufficient understanding by ordinary means (1.7).

- **Scripture interprets Scripture**  
  The infallible rule of interpretation is “the Scripture itself,” so that any obscure passage is to be understood in light of clearer passages on the same subject (1.9).

- **Final judge in controversies**  
  In all religious controversies the supreme judge is “no other but the Holy Scripture delivered by the Spirit,” and all decrees, opinions, and doctrines are to be examined and judged by it (1.10).

In short, the 1689 Confession articulates a classic Reformed Baptist expression of *sola Scriptura*: Scripture alone is the inspired, sufficient, clear, and final authority for all matters of faith and practice.

questions.response:
The 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith addresses the doctrine of God and the Trinity primarily in **Chapter 2** ("Of God and of the Holy Trinity"). Below is a clear summary of its teaching, drawn directly from the confession’s statements.

### 1. The Nature and Attributes of God
The confession affirms one living and true God who is:

- **Infinite, eternal, and immutable** in His being and perfections.
- **A pure spirit** — invisible, without body, parts, or passions.
- **Sovereign and self-sufficient** — He has all life, glory, goodness, and blessedness in and of Himself, and is the fountain of all being. All creatures depend on Him and owe Him worship and obedience.
- **Omnipotent, omniscient, and holy** — He works all things according to the counsel of His own will. His knowledge is infinite, infallible, and independent of the creature. He is most holy in all His counsels, works, and commands.
- **Moral character** — He is most loving, gracious, merciful, patient, abundant in goodness and truth, and forgiving; yet He is also just and will by no means clear the guilty. He hates all sin and is terrible in His judgments.

In short, God is completely independent of creation, absolutely sovereign over it, and worthy of all worship, service, and obedience from every creature.

### 2. The Doctrine of the Trinity
The confession teaches the classic Christian doctrine of the Trinity in unity:

- In the one divine essence there are **three persons** — the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
- These three persons are of **one substance, power, and eternity**.
- They are **distinguished** by their personal properties:
  - The Father is neither begotten nor proceeding.
  - The Son is eternally begotten of the Father.
  - The Holy Spirit eternally proceeds from the Father and the Son.
- Because they are infinite and without beginning, they constitute **one God**, not to be divided in nature or being, though distinguished by their personal relations and properties.

The confession emphasizes that this triune God is the proper object of all religious worship and the foundation of the believer’s communion with and dependence upon God.

### Summary Statement (from the Confession)
> “In this divine and infinite Being there are three subsistences, the Father, the Word or Son, and Holy Spirit, of one substance, power, and eternity, each having the whole divine essence, yet the essence undivided… which doctrine of the Trinity is the foundation of all our communion with God, and comfortable dependence on him.”

This chapter is intentionally aligned with earlier Reformed confessions (especially the Westminster Confession and the Savoy Declaration) while reflecting the Particular Baptist convictions of the late 17th century.

questions.response:
**The 1689 London Baptist Confession** (Second London Confession) addresses divine providence in **Chapter 5**, “Of Divine Providence.” It affirms a robust, comprehensive view of God’s sovereign governance over all things while carefully distinguishing God’s role from the authorship of sin. The main points are as follows:

### 1. God’s Universal and Sovereign Providence (5.1)
God, as the good Creator, upholds, directs, disposes, and governs every creature and event—from the greatest to the least—by His wise and holy providence. This extends to everything according to His infallible foreknowledge and the immutable counsel of His will, ultimately for His glory (praise of His wisdom, power, justice, goodness, and mercy).

### 2. No Chance or Mere Permission (5.2)
Nothing happens by chance or outside God’s providence. All events occur immutably and infallibly in relation to God’s decree (the first cause). At the same time, God ordinarily orders events to occur according to the nature of secondary causes—necessarily, freely, or contingently.

### 3. Use of Means (5.3)
In ordinary providence God works through means (secondary causes), yet He remains free to work without, above, or even against those means whenever He pleases.

### 4. Providence and Sin (5.4)
God’s providence extends even to the first fall and all other sinful acts of angels and men. This is not a bare permission; God wisely and powerfully bounds, orders, and governs sinful actions for His holy purposes. However, the sinfulness itself originates only from the creature—God, being perfectly holy, is neither the author nor approver of sin.

### 5. Providence Toward Believers (5.5)
God sometimes sovereignly leaves His own children to temptations and the corruptions of their hearts for wise and holy ends (chastisement, revealing remaining sin, increasing dependence on Him, greater watchfulness, etc.). Everything that befalls the elect is by God’s appointment for His glory and their good.

### 6. Providence Toward the Wicked (5.6)
Regarding the ungodly, God may judicially withhold grace, withdraw gifts, expose them to occasions of sin, and give them over to their own lusts, the world, and Satan, so that they harden themselves—even under means that soften others.

### 7. Special Care for the Church (5.7)
While God’s providence extends to all creatures, it operates in a special way toward His church, disposing all things for its good.

In short, the 1689 Confession presents God as the absolute, wise, and holy Governor of all events, working infallibly through secondary causes, yet remaining transcendent over them, while never being the source of moral evil. This chapter closely parallels the Westminster Confession (Chapter 5) but reflects the Particular Baptist convictions of the time.

questions.response:
The 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith addresses God’s covenant primarily in **Chapter 7** (“Of God’s Covenant”), with related statements in Chapters 6 (Of the Fall of Man), 8 (Of Christ the Mediator), and 11 (Of Justification). Its teaching can be summarized as follows:

### 1. The Necessity of Covenant
Because of the infinite distance between God and creatures, humanity could never have obtained eternal life by its own obedience apart from God’s voluntary condescension. God therefore deals with humanity by way of covenant (7.1).

### 2. Covenant of Works
God entered into a covenant of works with Adam in his state of innocence. Perfect, personal obedience was required, with the promise of life for obedience and death for disobedience (implicit in 7.1–2 and 6.1–2). Adam’s fall brought all humanity under the curse of that covenant.

### 3. Covenant of Grace
After the fall, God was pleased to make a single **covenant of grace**. In it he freely offers life and salvation to sinners through Jesus Christ, requiring faith in him. All who are ordained to eternal life are given the Holy Spirit so that they will believe (7.2).

### 4. Eternal Foundation
This covenant of grace is not a new arrangement invented in time; it is founded upon an eternal covenant transaction between the Father and the Son concerning the redemption of the elect (7.3).

### 5. Progressive Revelation
The covenant of grace was revealed gradually:
- First to Adam in the promise of the seed of the woman (Genesis 3:15).
- Then through further steps in the Old Testament.
- Finally brought to full clarity in the New Testament (7.3).

All who have ever been saved since the fall have been saved by the grace of this one covenant, not by the covenant of works (which fallen humanity is now incapable of fulfilling).

### Summary
The 1689 Confession teaches a **two-covenant** framework (works and grace) while emphasizing that the covenant of grace is one and the same in substance from Genesis 3 onward, rooted in eternity, and administered differently before and after Christ. It rejects any notion of multiple, substantially different covenants of grace.

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about christ the mediator?
questions.reference_answer: It pleased God in his eternal purpose, to chuse and ordain the Lord Jesus his only begotten Son, according to the Covenant made between them both, to be the Mediator between God and Man; the Prophet, Priest and King; Head and Saviour of his Church, the heir of all things, and judge of the world: Unto whom he did from all Eternity give a people to be his seed, and to be by him in time redeemed, called, justified, sanctified, and glorified. The Son of God, the second Person in the Holy Trinity, being very and eternal God, the brightness of the Fathers glory, of one substance and equal with him: who made the World, who upholdeth and governeth all things he hath made: did when the fullness of time was come take unto him mans nature, with all the Essential properties, and common infirmities thereof, yet without sin: being conceived by the Holy Spirit in the Womb of the Virgin Mary, the Holy Spirit coming down upon her, and the power of the most High overshadowing her, and so was made of a Woman, of the Tribe of Judah, of the Seed of Abraham, and David according to the Scriptures: So that two whole, perfect, and distinct natures, were inseparably joined together in one Person: without conversion, composition, or confusion: which Person is very God, and very Man; yet one Christ, the only Mediator between God and Man. The Lord Jesus in his humane nature thus united to the divine, in the Person of the Son, was sanctified, and anointed with the Holy Spirit, above measure; having in him all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge; in whom it pleased the Father that all fullness should dwell: To the end that being holy, harmless, undefiled, and full of Grace, and Truth, he might be throughly furnished to execute the office of a Mediator, and Surety; which office he took not upon himself, but was thereunto called by his Father; who also put all power and judgement in his hand, and gave him Commandement to execute the same. This office the Lord Jesus did most willingly undertake, which that he might discharge he was made under the Law, and did perfectly fulfill it, and underwent the punishment due to us, which we should have born and suffered, being made Sin and a Curse for us: enduring most grievous sorrows in his Soul; and most painful sufferings in his body; was crucified, and died, and remained in the state of the dead; yet saw no corruption: on the third day he arose from the dead, with the same body in which he suffered; with which he also ascended into heaven: and there sitteth at the right hand of his Father, making intercession; and shall return to judge Men and Angels, at the end of the World. The Lord Jesus by his perfect obedience and sacrifice of himself, which he through the Eternal Spirit once offered up unto God, hath fully satisfied the Justice of God, procured reconciliation, and purchased an Everlasting inheritance in the Kingdom of Heaven, for all those whom the Father hath given unto him. Although the price of Redemption was not actually paid by Christ, till after his Incarnation, yet the vertue, efficacy, and benefit thereof were communicated to the Elect in all ages successively, from the beginning of the World, in and by those Promises, Types, and Sacrifices, wherein he was revealed, and signified to be the Seed of the Woman, which should bruise the Serpents head; and the Lamb slain from the foundation of the World: Being the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever. Christ in the work of Mediation acteth according to both natures, by each nature doing that which is proper to it self; yet by reason of the Unity of the Person, that which is proper to one nature, is sometimes in Scripture attributed to the Person denominated by the other nature. To all those for whom Christ hath obtained eternal redemption, he doth certainly, and effectually apply, and communicate the same; making intercession for them, uniting them to himself by his spirit, revealing unto them, in and by the word, the mystery of salvation; perswading them to believe, and obey; governing their hearts by his word and spirit, and overcoming all their enemies by his Almighty power, and wisdom; in such manner, and wayes as are most consonant to his wonderful, and unsearchable dispensation; and all of free, and absolute Grace, without any condition foreseen in them, to procure it. This office of Mediator between God and Man, is proper onely to Christ, who is the Prophet, Priest, and King of the Church of God; and may not be either in whole, or any part thereof transfer'd from him to any other. This number and order of Offices is necessary; for in respect of our ignorance, we stand in need of his prophetical Office; and in respect of our alienation from God, and imperfection of the best of our services, we need his Priestly office, to reconcile us, and present us acceptable unto God: and in respect our averseness, and utter inability to return to God, and for our rescue, and security from our spiritual adversaries, we need his Kingly office, to convince, subdue, draw, uphold, deliver, and preserve us to his Heavenly Kingdome.

questions.response:
The 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith addresses Christ as Mediator primarily in **Chapter 8** (“Of Christ the Mediator”), with related statements in Chapters 7, 11, 12, 14, and 30. Its teaching is strongly Reformed, echoing the Westminster Confession while making modest Baptist adjustments (e.g., on the scope of redemption and the church). Here is a concise summary of its doctrine:

### 1. Eternal Appointment
God, from all eternity, was pleased to choose and ordain the Lord Jesus, his only-begotten Son, to be the Mediator between God and man (8.1). Christ was set apart and anointed with the Holy Spirit for this office before the foundation of the world.

### 2. Two Natures in One Person
In the fullness of time, the Son assumed a true human nature—being conceived by the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin Mary—while remaining truly God. These two whole, perfect, and distinct natures (divine and human) are inseparably joined in one person without confusion, conversion, or composition. He is therefore truly God and truly man, yet one Christ (8.2).

### 3. Offices
Christ executes the offices of Prophet, Priest, and King, both in his state of humiliation and exaltation (8.1, 8.3). As Prophet he reveals God’s will; as Priest he offers himself as a sacrifice and intercedes; as King he rules and defends his people.

### 4. Work of Mediation
- He perfectly fulfilled the law and offered himself up as a once-for-all sacrifice of infinite value and efficacy (8.4–5).
- By his obedience and death he purchased reconciliation, eternal redemption, and an everlasting inheritance for all those the Father had given him.
- He rose bodily, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father, where he continually makes intercession for his people (8.4).
- His mediation is effectual only for the elect; he does not redeem all humanity indiscriminately (8.5, 8.8).

### 5. Exclusivity
Christ alone is the Mediator; no other person or angel can fulfill this role (8.9). All saving grace comes through him alone.

### 6. Application to Believers
Those who are effectually called receive justification, adoption, sanctification, and all saving benefits through the mediation of Christ (Chapters 11–13). His work is the sole ground of the believer’s assurance and perseverance.

In short, the 1689 Confession presents Christ as the eternal, divinely appointed Mediator who, in one person, unites full deity and true humanity, perfectly accomplishes redemption for the elect through his prophetic, priestly, and kingly work, and continues to intercede until he returns to judge the world.

questions.response:
**The 1689 London Baptist Confession** addresses effectual calling primarily in **Chapter 10** ("Of Effectual Calling"). It presents a thoroughly Reformed, monergistic view: God sovereignly and irresistibly calls the elect to salvation by His Word and Spirit, apart from any foreseen merit or cooperation in the sinner.
### Key Teachings (summarized from the Confession)
1. **God’s Sovereign Initiative** (Paragraph 1)
 Those whom God has predestinated to life are effectually called in His appointed time “by His Word and Spirit” out of sin and death into grace and salvation in Christ. This involves:
 - Spiritually enlightening their minds to understand the things of God.
 - Removing the heart of stone and giving a heart of flesh.
 - Renewing their wills and “by His almighty power determining them to that which is good.”
 - Effectually drawing them to Christ, yet in such a way that they come *most freely*, being made willing by grace.
2. **Grace Alone, Not Human Ability** (Paragraph 2)
 Effectual calling flows from “God’s free and special grace alone,” not from anything foreseen in man or any power in the creature. The sinner is “wholly passive” while dead in sins until quickened by the Holy Spirit. Only then is he enabled to answer the call—by the same power that raised Christ from the dead.
3. **Elect Infants and the Incapable** (Paragraph 3)
 Elect infants dying in infancy (and all other elect persons incapable of being outwardly called by the Word) are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works “when, and where, and how He pleaseth.”
4. **The Non-Elect** (Paragraph 4)
 Those not elect may hear the outward call of the Word and experience common operations of the Spirit, yet they are not effectually drawn by the Father. Consequently they neither can nor will come to Christ and cannot be saved. The same applies to those who reject the Christian religion, no matter how moral they may be.
### Summary of the Confession’s Doctrine
Effectual calling is the *irresistible*, regenerating work of God that infallibly brings the elect to saving faith in Christ. It is monergistic (God alone acts to make the dead sinner alive and willing), grounded solely in divine election and grace, and distinct from the general outward call of the gospel that many hear but do not savingly respond to.
This chapter closely parallels the Westminster Confession (Chapter 10) while reflecting the Particular Baptist convictions of the late 17th century.

questions.response:
**The 1689 London Baptist Confession** teaches justification in Chapter 11 (“Of Justification”). Its doctrine is thoroughly Reformed and forensic, closely paralleling the Westminster Confession while making a few Baptist adjustments. The main points are:

- **Forensic act of God’s free grace**  
  Justification is not an infusion of righteousness into the sinner but a legal declaration in which God pardons sin and accounts the sinner righteous on the basis of Christ’s obedience and satisfaction (11.1). It is “not by infusing righteousness into them, but by pardoning their sins, and by accounting and accepting their persons as righteous.”

- **Grounded solely in Christ’s work**  
  The righteousness imputed is Christ’s whole obedience—both his active obedience to the law and his passive obedience in suffering—reckoned to the believer (11.1, 3). Nothing done by the believer contributes to the ground of justification.

- **Received by faith alone**  
  Faith is the alone instrument of justification. It is “not of themselves” but is the gift of God, and it does not justify because it is a work or because it produces any inherent righteousness (11.1–2).

- **Eternal decree, personal application in time**  
  God decreed from eternity to justify the elect, and Christ accomplished their justification in his death and resurrection. Nevertheless, the elect “are not justified personally, until the Holy Spirit doth in due time actually apply Christ unto them” (11.4). Thus there is an eternal aspect in God’s purpose and a temporal aspect in the believer’s experience.

- **Permanent and complete**  
  Justification is a once-for-all act that can never be lost or repeated. Those who are justified are also freed from the law as a covenant of works for justification, though they remain under the moral law as a rule of life (11.5–6).

- **Results**  
  Justification brings peace with God, access to grace, and the hope of glory. It is accompanied by the Spirit’s witness and produces good works as its necessary fruit, though those works play no part in the justifying verdict itself (11.1, 6).

In short, the 1689 Confession presents justification as a gracious, forensic imputation of Christ’s righteousness received by faith alone, decreed from eternity yet applied personally at conversion, and permanently securing the believer’s standing before God.

questions.response:
The 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith addresses the perseverance of the saints in **Chapter 17** ("Of the Perseverance of the Saints"). It teaches that all true believers—those whom God has accepted in Christ, effectually called, and sanctified by His Spirit—will certainly persevere in grace to the end and be eternally saved. They cannot totally or finally fall away from a state of grace.

### Key Points from the Confession

- **Certainty of perseverance**: Those truly regenerated and united to Christ "can neither totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace, but shall certainly persevere therein to the end, and be eternally saved" (17.1). This is grounded not in human free will or effort, but in:
  - The immutability of God’s decree of election.
  - The efficacy of Christ’s intercession and merit.
  - The abiding presence and work of the Holy Spirit.
  - The nature of the covenant of grace.

- **Sin and restoration**: Believers may fall into grievous sins through temptation, corruption, or neglect, and thereby grieve the Spirit, impair their comforts, and bring temporal judgments on themselves. However, they will be renewed again unto repentance and preserved from utter apostasy (17.2–3).

- **Divine preservation**: The saints’ continuance in faith depends wholly on God’s sovereign power and faithfulness to His promises, not on their own strength. This doctrine is meant to encourage humility, watchfulness, and diligence in the use of means of grace (such as the Word, prayer, and the ordinances).

In short, the 1689 Confession affirms a Calvinistic view of perseverance: genuine saints are kept by God’s power through faith unto final salvation, even though they may stumble and sin along the way. This teaching closely parallels the Westminster Confession (Chapter 17) but is framed within a Baptist understanding of the church and baptism.

questions.response:
The 1689 London Baptist Confession addresses the Last Judgment primarily in **Chapter 32** (“Of the Last Judgment”). Its teaching can be summarized as follows:

### 1. A definite future day of judgment
God has appointed a specific day on which He will judge the world in righteousness through Jesus Christ, to whom all authority to judge has been given by the Father (32.1). On that day:
- Both fallen angels and every human being who has ever lived will appear before Christ’s judgment seat.
- Each person will give an account of their thoughts, words, and deeds and will be recompensed according to what they have done in the body, whether good or evil.

### 2. Purpose of the judgment
The judgment serves to display the glory of God’s attributes (32.2):
- **Mercy** — manifested in the eternal salvation of the elect.
- **Justice** — manifested in the eternal damnation of the reprobate (those who are wicked and disobedient).

At the judgment the righteous will enter “everlasting life” and receive “fulness of joy and glory” in the presence of the Lord, while the wicked “shall be cast aside into everlasting torments” and suffer “everlasting destruction, from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power.”

### 3. Practical implications
Because Scripture clearly affirms that such a day will come, believers are to be “certainly persuaded” of it (32.3). This certainty has two effects:
- It deters all people from sin.
- It gives greater consolation to the godly in their present sufferings.

At the same time, the exact timing of the day remains hidden from humanity so that people will not fall into carnal security but will instead live in constant watchfulness, always ready for Christ’s return.

In short, the 1689 Confession presents the Last Judgment as a future, universal, and public event carried out by Christ that vindicates God’s justice and mercy, issues in eternal destinies, and calls believers to holy vigilance.

questions.question: Does the fall affect every part of human nature?
questions.reference_answer: The fall corrupted every faculty of man Mind, will, and affections are all affected This is total depravity — not utter depravity

questions.response:
**Yes, in classical Christian theology the Fall is understood to have corrupted every dimension of human nature.**
The doctrine of original sin, articulated most sharply by Augustine and later by the Reformed confessions, holds that Adam’s disobedience introduced a comprehensive disorder: the intellect is darkened, the will is enslaved to sinful desires, the emotions are disordered, and even the body is subject to decay and death. No faculty remains untouched; humans retain the image of God in a defaced form, but they do not possess any moral or spiritual neutrality from which they could initiate their own recovery.
This is not the claim that every person is maximally wicked at every moment, but that sin has penetrated the root of human faculties so that no part functions as it was originally created to do. The mind suppresses truth (Romans 1), the heart is deceitful (Jeremiah 17:9), and the will cannot submit to God’s law apart from regenerating grace (Romans 8:7–8). Hence the traditional label “total depravity.”
Outside that theological framework the question has no direct referent; evolutionary biology and psychology describe persistent human limitations—cognitive biases, status-seeking, tribal aggression, mortality—without invoking a primordial historical rupture. Those accounts treat the same phenomena as by-products of selection pressures rather than inherited guilt. Within the Christian story, however, the answer is affirmative: the Fall is total in scope though not absolute in degree.

questions.response:
This question lies at the heart of longstanding debates in Christian theology, particularly between Calvinist and Arminian traditions, with answers depending on how one interprets Scripture, divine sovereignty, and human responsibility.

## Core Positions
- **Calvinist view (unconditional election)**: God elects individuals for salvation solely according to His sovereign will and pleasure, not based on any foreseen faith or merit in them. Passages such as Ephesians 1:4-5 ("He chose us in him before the foundation of the world") and Romans 9:11-13 (Jacob and Esau chosen before birth or actions) are cited to argue that election precedes and causes faith, rather than responding to it. Faith is seen as a gift granted by God to the elect (Ephesians 2:8-9).
- **Arminian view (conditional election)**: God chooses to save those whom He foreknows will respond in faith. Romans 8:29 ("those whom he foreknew he also predestined") and 1 Peter 1:1-2 ("elect... according to the foreknowledge of God") are emphasized, with foreknowledge understood as God's awareness of future free choices. Election is thus conditioned on faith, preserving genuine human responsibility.
- **Other perspectives**: Molinism attempts a middle ground by proposing that God uses "middle knowledge" of what free creatures would do in any circumstance to arrange salvation accordingly. Some Reformed thinkers reject foreseen faith as undermining grace, while open theists question exhaustive foreknowledge altogether.

## Key Scriptural and Logical Tensions
- Texts like Acts 13:48 ("as many as were appointed to eternal life believed") favor divine initiative preceding belief.
- Passages stressing human response, such as John 3:16 or 2 Peter 3:9, are read by conditional election advocates as indicating that faith is the condition God honors.
- Philosophically, unconditional election raises questions about fairness and genuine love, while conditional election raises questions about whether salvation remains entirely by grace or subtly incorporates human contribution.

Interpretations ultimately rest on broader commitments about God's nature, the extent of human depravity, and the mechanics of foreknowledge. No empirical resolution exists; conclusions follow from one's systematic reading of the biblical data.

questions.response:
The question of whether God's election of individuals to salvation is conditional or unconditional stands as one of the most enduring divides in Christian theology, particularly between Reformed and Arminian traditions.

## Unconditional Election
This view holds that God's choice of individuals for salvation rests entirely on His sovereign will and purpose, without dependence on any foreseen faith, works, or merit in the person elected. Proponents argue that human depravity renders any condition impossible, making election an act of pure grace.

- Key arguments emphasize divine sovereignty and the impossibility of earning or contributing to salvation. If election depended on human response, it would undermine grace and introduce works-based elements.
- Scriptural support often includes Romans 9:11-13, where God's choice of Jacob over Esau occurs before birth "so that God's purpose of election might continue," and Ephesians 1:4-5, describing election "before the foundation of the world" according to God's will.
- This position aligns with the broader framework of total depravity and irresistible grace, ensuring salvation cannot be credited to human initiative.

## Conditional Election
The alternative perspective maintains that God elects individuals based on His foreknowledge of their faith or response to the gospel. Election remains gracious because faith itself is enabled by prevenient grace, yet it incorporates a human condition.

- Key arguments focus on God's justice and relational nature, suggesting unconditional election risks portraying God as arbitrary or inconsistent with passages stressing human responsibility to believe.
- Scriptural support frequently cites 1 Peter 1:1-2, linking election to "foreknowledge of God the Father," and Romans 8:29, where those God foreknew He also predestined. Advocates interpret foreknowledge as relational awareness rather than mere prediction.
- This view integrates with teachings on resistible grace and the universal offer of salvation, preserving meaningful human agency.

## Additional Considerations
Other frameworks exist, such as corporate election, where God chooses a people (the church) rather than isolated individuals, or middle knowledge approaches that seek to reconcile sovereignty with genuine contingency. Interpretations ultimately depend on broader commitments to how Scripture balances divine initiative and human response. No single position resolves every tension without further theological assumptions.
